# v10.1.0

`Result<T>` now derives from `Result`, results can carry several errors, and the library gains the railway combinators (`Map`, `Bind`, `Ensure`, `Tap`, `TapError`) with async support, plus implicit conversions for returning values and errors directly.

> **This release contains breaking changes.** Arcanic.Result versions follow the .NET major version (10.x for .NET 10), so breaking changes can ship in a minor release. Read the migration notes below before upgrading from 10.0.0.

## Breaking changes

### `Result<T>` derives from `Result`

Previously `Result` derived from `Result<Result>`. That exposed a meaningless `Value` and value-based `Match` overloads on untyped results. The hierarchy is now reversed, so every `Result<T>` is a `Result`, and code that only needs success or failure (logging, pipeline behaviors, `Result.Combine`) can treat all results the same way.

### Returning `Result.Failure(error)` from a method returning `Result<T>` no longer compiles

C# does not allow user-defined conversions from a base class, so the implicit `Result` → `Result<T>` conversion is gone (error CS0029).

```csharp
// Before (10.0.0)
public Result<User> Find(int id) =>
    user is null ? Result.Failure(UserErrors.NotFound) : Result.Success(user);

// After (10.1.0): return the error directly...
public Result<User> Find(int id) =>
    user is null ? UserErrors.NotFound : user;

// ...or use the typed factory
return Result.Failure<User>(UserErrors.NotFound);
```

### `Result.Value` is removed

`Result` no longer has a `Value` property. In 10.0.0 it always threw, so code that compiled against it never worked; remove those calls.

### Value-based `Match` on `Result` is removed

In 10.0.0, `Match(value => ..., error => ...)` compiled on an untyped `Result` and passed `null` as the value. Those overloads no longer exist; use `Match(() => ..., error => ...)`.

### Invalid errors are rejected

- `Result.Failure(null)` (and the implicit conversion from a `null` error) now throws `ArgumentNullException`. It used to create a failure whose `Error` was `null`.
- An error with an empty code and description is now a valid failure. It used to be mistaken for `Error.None` and throw.

## New features

### Implicit conversions

Return a value or an error directly from a method returning `Result<T>`:

```csharp
public Result<int> Parse(string input) =>
    int.TryParse(input, out var n) ? n : Error.Validation("INVALID_NUMBER", "Not a number");
```

C# does not apply user-defined conversions from interface types, so for results like `Result<IEnumerable<T>>` use `Result.Success(value)`.

### Multiple errors

- `Errors`: every error of a failed result, in order (empty on success). `Error` is still the first one, so single-error code is unaffected.
- `Result.Failure(IEnumerable<Error>)` and `Result.Failure<T>(IEnumerable<Error>)`.
- `Result.Combine(...)` merges results (typed and untyped) and collects every error.

### Railway combinators

`Map`, `Bind`, `Ensure`, `Tap` and `TapError` on `Result` and `Result<T>`. Each runs only on success, and otherwise passes the failure along with all of its errors.

### Async pipelines

- The same names on `Task<Result<T>>` / `Task<Result>` take synchronous functions.
- `MapAsync`, `BindAsync`, `EnsureAsync` and `TapAsync` take asynchronous functions.
- `Match` works on a task.

```csharp
string message = await users.FindAsync(id)
    .Ensure(user => user.IsActive, UserErrors.Inactive)
    .BindAsync(user => mailer.SendWelcomeAsync(user))
    .Match(() => "Welcome email sent", error => error.Description);
```

### `Result.Failure<T>(error)`

A typed failure factory, useful where the target type cannot be inferred.

## Multi-targeting

Targets .NET 8, .NET 9, and .NET 10.
